caseno: Writ Petition Nos. 6433-39 of 2003 and 5950 of 2003
lawyer:
Mahbubur Rahman with Ashik Al Jalil, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 

Fida M Kamal, Additional Attorney-General with Syeda Afsar Jahan, Assistant Attorney-General—For the Respondents.
parties:
Cab Express (BD) Ltd ------- Petitioner
vs
Commissioner of Customs and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J: In all these Rules the question raised is whether assessment of customs duty on the basis of an SRO issued subsequent to the opening of the Letters of Credit is without lawful authority. Since common questions of law and fact are involved in all these Rules the same are taken up together for hearing and disposed of by this one judgment.

2. The case of the petitioners in all these writ petitions is that, they opened their respective Letters of Credit being inspired by SRO No. 56-Ain /99 /1780/Cus dated 16-3-1999 issued under section 19 of the Customs Act, 1969 and section 14(1) of the VAT Act, 1991 by the National Board of Revenue allowing import of Taxi Cabs upon fulfilment of certain conditions incorporated in the said SRO at an exemption of customs duty above 7.5%. The petitioners pursuant to the said SRO upon fulfilling all the conditions incorporated therein imported the vehicles as mentioned in their respective Writ Petitions vide their respective Letters of Credit from India. The petitioners on different dates from 19th March, 2003 to 3rd July, 2003 got their consignments inspected by the approved PSI agents. On arrival of all the consignment at Benapole land port the petitioners submitted their concerned Bills of Entry along with all necessary papers on different dates from 2-9-2003 to 13-10-2003 for assessment of customs duty and release of the goods on the basis of the aforesaid SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999.

3. The writ petitioners in their respective petitions stated that earlier the customs authority for unknown reasons refused to accept the Bills of Entry from the importers of taxicab and, as such, delay was caused in submitting the Bills of Entry for release of the vehicles. However, upon receipt of the said Bills of Entry the customs authority by their impugned orders, demanded customs duty and other charges on the basis of SRO No. 158- Ain /2003 /2010/Cus dated 12-6-2003 and refused to assess and release the vehicles on the basis of SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999.

4. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the orders of the customs authority the petitioners obtained these Rules in all these writ petitions.

5. The respondent No. 1 i.e. the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Benapole. Jessore entered appearance and contested these Rules by filing affidavit-in-opposition through the learned Assistant Attorney-General, The contention of the respondents are that the writ petitioner's goods arrived at Benapole land port between 8-5-2003, to 12-5-2003 i.e. 1 (one) month and 4 (four) days before the relevant SRO No. 56 of 1999 was amended by SRO No. 158 dated 12-6-2003. Although the petitioners had ample time to present the Bills of Entry before SRO No.158 was issued but the petitioners submitted their respective Bills of Entry subsequent to issuance of SRO No. 158 of 2003, as such, the petitioners' goods are liable to be assessed on the basis of the said SRO which was prevalent on the date of submission of their Bills of Entry as contemplated in section 30 of the Customs Act 1969. In the present cases since the rate of duty was subsequently amended by SRO No. 158 of 2003 issued on 12-6-2003 and the Bills of Entry were presented on 21-6-2003 i.e. after the said SRO came into force, duty should be assessed on the basis of the subsequent SRO No. 158. Further contention of the said respondent is that the importers were probably waiting for a favourable change in the budget but when they found the budget unfavourable they took the plea that they are entitled to get benefit of the previous SRO since the Letters of Credit have been opened under the said SRO by which a vested right has already been created in their favour. The petitioners have not submitted their Bills of Entry prior to the amendment of SRO No. 56 by SRO No. 158 dated 12-6-2003 though the goods arrived much earlier and, as such, they cannot claim any vested right. The contention of the respondent is that to claim a vested right the petitioners have a vested duty of submitting the Bills of Entry at the earlier possible date subsequent to arrival of the goods in Bangladesh. It is contended that the petitioners had sufficient time prior to issuance of the amended SRO No.158 dated 12-6-2003 but they did not avail the opportunity of submitting their respective Bills of Entry and, as such, they cannot take the plea of vested right now.

6. Mr Mahbubur Rahman, the learned Senior Advocate appearing with Mr Ashik Al Jalil, the learned Advocate for the petitioners in all these writ petitions, submits that the impugned orders passed by the customs authority are illegal and without lawful authority as the import was made pursuant to the special benefit granted by SRO No. 56 of 1999 to the importers of taxicab for the purpose of meeting the urgent cry of the public in the public transport sector in the Metropolitan area because of the vacuum created by banning two strokes 3-wheeler auto rickshaws plying in the Metropolis and because of the rapid growth of the population in those areas. Such facilities were given to the importers by the said SRO to meet the growing public demand in the transport sector. He further submits that in the said SRO the authority has incorporated certain terms and conditions which were required to be fulfilled for availing the facilities for exemption of customs duty granted in the said SRO. According to him, upon completion of all the terms and conditions of the SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999 and the goods having been inspected by the approved PSI agents, who found the same to be in accordance with the requirements and the goods having reached Bangladesh prior to issuance of the subsequent SRO No. 158 of 2003 but the petitioner being unable to present their respective Bills of Entry because of the refusal to accept the same by the customs authority for the reasons best known to them and because the customs authority having received the Bills of Entry in accordance with section 79(2) of the Act, now they cannot deny the benefit of SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999 to the petitioners. According to him the subsequent SRO having reduced the rate of exemption and putting a bottom line in the CC of the taxicab the same is not at all applicable for the consignments which reached Bangladesh much earlier than the issuance of the subsequent SRO. In this respect he relied on the decisions in Hannan case, reported 42 DLR (AD) 167. Ahmed Hossain's case reported in 48 DLR (AD) 199 and Khairul Bashar's case reported in 50 DLR 225. Accordingly, he submits that the importers upon fulfilling all the requirements of SRO No. 56 of 1999 having opened the Letters of Credit and having brought the goods in the Benapole Land Port prior to issuance of SRO No. 158 of 2003 a vested right has been created to get their goods assessed under the earlier SRO. He submits that the authority having promised by SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999 to give certain facilities to the importers upon fulfilling the terms and conditions incorporated therein, now they cannot go back upon it i.e. on their promise, as the same is binding upon them and such binding is termed as promissory estopped. Mr Rahman submits that his view is fully supported by the decision given in the case of Commissioner of Customs and others vs Monohor Ali and others reported in 2003 BLD (AD) 59 = 8 BLC (AD) 87. While making his submission Mr Rahman drew our attention to a judgment delivered by one of the Benches of this Court, in Writ Petition No. 4603 of 2003 (wherein one of us is a party) and submits that upon accepting the view taken in Monohor Ali's case their Lordships made the Rule absolute. Accordingly, he submits that the petitioners in all these Rules being on the same footing are entitled to get the same result.

7. Mr Rahman in addition to his above submissions emphatically submitted on section 19 of the Customs Act. According to him, in all these Rules the questions raised relate to exemption of duty granted under section 19 of the Customs Act. In this regard he further submits that under no circumstances the date of submission of Bills of Entry will be the relevant factor for assessment of customs duty because SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999 was issued in special circumstances for special purpose on public interest and gave some special terms and conditions to be fulfilled to get benefit of the said SRO. The actions of the importers upon fulfilling all the terms and conditions under such special circumstances entitles them to get the facilities and incentives given in the said SRO. Lastly, Mr Rahman submits that upon fulfilment of all the terms and conditions incorporated in the concerned SRO No. 56 of 1999 the taxicabs imported by the petitioners now cannot be used for any other purpose other than the purpose for which those were manufactured and imported. Accordingly, he submits that at least for ends of justice the petitioners should be allowed to avail the facilities of exemption granted in the said SRO No. 56 of 1999.

8. On the other hand, Mr Fida M Kamal, the learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for respondent No. 1, submits that since all the Bills of Entry in all the writ petitions were submitted after the amended SRO No. 158 dated 12-6-2003 came into force the customs authority, according to section 30 of the Act, rightly passed the impugned orders refusing to assess customs duty on the basis of earlier SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999. He next submits that the Assistant Commissioner issued all the impugned orders, which are under challenge in all the writ petitions, so the alternative remedy in the form of appeal was the appropriate forum available for all the writ petitioners and having not availed the forum of appeal all these writ petitions are not maintainable. Thirdly, he submits that the price certified by the approved PSI agents are not binding upon the customs authority because the PSI facilities are given under section 25A of the Customs Act and in all these cases the matters relate to exemption of duty under section 19 of the Act. So, the question of availing CRF facilities provided under section 25A does not attract these cases. According to him, the CRF certificate is not in dispute in these cases rather, the question of exemption and the rate of duty are in dispute in all these rules so under no circumstances the Monohor Ali case will be applicable. According to him, since Monohor Ali case is not applicable, the question of vested right is also not a matter to be decided in these cases, mere opening of Letters of Credit during the subsistence of the previous SRO, will not create any vested right so far the applicability of the rate of duty is concerned. According to him, so long section 30 read with section 30A of the Customs Act with a non-obstante clause subsists, passing of the impugned orders are justified and, as such, the rate of duty applicable on the basis of the rate prevailing on the date of submissions of the Bills of Entry, regardless of the date of opening of the Letters of Credit, should be applicable in the present cases and, as such, the impugned orders have been rightly passed. Referring to Monohor Ali's case reported in 2003 BLD (AD) 59 = 8 BLC (AD) 87,the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that it is clearly distinguishable on the facts as determined in Para 17 of the said decision. Both sections 30A and 25A came into operation of 1-7-1995, but in section 30A there is nothing to suggest that it excluded the operation of section 25A of the Customs Act. At the present moment section 25A stands amended and does not contain the non-obstante clause and, as such, Monohor Ali's case is not applicable in the fact and circumstances of the present rules. Under such circumstances he submits that since section 30A contains non-obstante clause it obviously overrides all other sections of the Customs Act including sections 19, 25 and 30. Thus the petitioners under all circumstances are liable to pay customs duty at the rate prevalent on the date of submission of the Bills of Entry.

9. Replying to petitioners' submissions on Hannan's case reported in 42 DLR the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that the said case was decided for limited purpose giving special emphasis on special circumstances for importing sugar. According to him, in 1984 when there was scarcity of sugar in the country the Government decided and issued Gazette Notification for import of sugar giving incentive to the importer by a concessional rate and specifying the time limit for import of the same with condition to make the shipment within 15 days, but the view taken therein is clearly distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the instant cases. Thus the importers in the present cases are liable to pay the customs duty prevalent on the date of submission of their Bills of Entry. According to him, the exemption granted by SRO No. 56 of 1999 was in force till the subsequent SRO No.158 was issued, whereby the exemption previously granted was withdrawn in certain aspect. Accordingly, the rate of duty will be as per subsequent SRO No. 158 of 2003 which was prevailing when the Bills of Entry were submitted. On elaborating this point, the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that the government has the power to exempt the rate of duty under section 19 of the Customs Act, but proviso to that section says that the same cannot be done more than once in the year so as to increase the rate of duty. Thus by exercising the power under section 19 the rate of duty as fixed by SRO No. 56 of 1999 being amended by subsequent SRO No. 158 of 2002 is a lawful exercise of power. He submits that SRO No. 56 came into force in 1999 and SRO No. 158 came into force in 2003. So the proviso to section 19 is also not violated as the change was made nearly after 4 years. According to him, the Government vis-a-vis the customs authority, can fix the customs duty within the ceiling and also the exemption can be varied to any extent within that ceiling but once a year. Thus he submits, section 19 empowers the authority to exempt the customs duties and sections 30 and 30A empowers the authority to realise the same on the basis of the rate prevalent on the date of presentation of the Bills of Entry. In support of his contentions, he relied on the case of Selim (Md) vs Collector of Customs and others reported in 54 DLR 287 and Mizanur Rahman case in 52 DLR (AD) 149.

10. Lastly, the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that the unreported 'decision of this Court in Writ Petition No. 4603 of 2003, judgment delivered on 27-8-2003, wherein one of us is a party, their Lordships wrongly relied on Monohor Ali's case and made the Rule absolute which, according to him is not applicable to any of these cases. His contention is that the pleadings and submissions made in these Rules were neither placed nor considered in the said writ petition. The said judgment is per in curium and, as such, has no binding effect. He relied on the decision reported in 10 BLT 104 = 5 BLC 528 (Abul Kalam Khan vs Reaz Morshed and others). In consolidating his submissions, the learned Additional Attorney-General pointed out that the impugned orders, challenged in these writ petitions, not being the final order all these petitions are pre-mature. Without any final decision being passed shelter of law cannot be sought under Article 102 of the Constitution. The petitioners rather had alternative remedy in appeal under section 193 of the Act. Without exhausting the statutory alternative remedy the instant writ petitions are not maintainable.

11. We have heard the learned Advocates at length and perused all the writ petitions along with the papers annexed thereto, the supplementary affidavits, affidavits-in-opposition and also the affidavits-in-reply. It appears to us that the questions raised in all these Rules are whether exemption under section 19 of the Customs Act and section 14 of the VAT Act as granted by SRO No. 56 of 1999, will be applicable in the cases where the Letters of Credit were opened and inspections were held prior to amendment of the said exemption or at the amended rate provided by subsequent SRO No. 158 of 2003 which was prevalent on the date of presentation of Bill of Entry. It appears that both section 19 of the Customs Act and section 14 of the VAT Act deal with the power of the government to exempt customs duty, tax and supplementary duties on certain goods imported by the importers. Now the question is, whether such exemption granted by SRO No. 56 of 1999 will be applicable in the present case. To resolve the point raised in these rules, let us see the relevant provisions of law and the concerned SRO. Section 19 of the Customs Act reads as follow:

"19. General power to exempt from customs duties:—(1) If the Government is satisfied after consultation with the Board, that it is necessary in the public interest to do so, it may, subject to such conditions, limitations or restrictions, if any, as it thinks fit to impose by notification in the official Gazette, exempt any goods imported into or exported from, (Bangladesh) or into, or from any specified port or station or area therein, from the whole or any part of the customs duties chargeable thereon.

Provided that if, in a financial year, exemption under this sub-section is given in respect of any goods the rate of duty cannot be changed more than once in that year so as to increase that rate.

(2) An exemption granted under sub-section (1) shall be effective from the date mentioned in the notification issued under that sub-section."

SRO No. 56 of 1999 under which the Letters of Credit were opened and the goods imported, reads as follows:

“প্ৰজ্ঞাপন

ঢাকা, ২-১২-১৪০৫ বাংলা/১৬ই মার্চ ১৯৯৯ ইংরেজি ৷

নং-এস আর ও ৫৬ অইিন/৯৯/১৭৮০/ণ্ডল্ক ৷ Customs  Act, 1969 এর (IV of 1969) section 1 এবং মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ (১৯৯১ সনের ২২নং আইন) এর ধারা ১৪(১) এর প্রদত্ত ক্ষমতাবলে সরকার জাতীয় রাজস্ব বোর্ডের সহিত পরামর্শক্রমে জনস্বার্থে অত্র বিভাগের ২৯শে জ্যেষ্ঠ, ১৪০৪ বাংলা মোতাবেক ১২ই জুন, ১৯৯৭ ইংরেজি তারিখের প্রজ্ঞাপন এস আর ও নং ১৫১ আইন/৯৭/১৭০৯/শুল্ক রহিত করিয়া উক্ত Act এর FIRST SCHEDULE এ বর্ণিত Heading No. 87,03 এর বিপরীতে আমদানিকৃত মটর গাড়ির উপর আরোপিত আমদানি শুস্কের যে পরিমাণ শুল্ক মূল্য ভিত্তিক শতকরা ৭.৫% এর অতিরিক্ত হয় সেই পরিমাণ আমদানি শুল্ক এবং সমুদয় সম্পূরক শুল্ক, নিম্ন বর্ণিত শর্ত

সাপেক্ষে, মওকুফ করিল, যথাঃ-

(১ ) “ট্যাক্সিক্যাব হিসাবে ব্যবহারের লক্ষ্যে আমদানিকৃত অনূর্ধ্ব ২০০০ সি সি ক্ষমতা সম্পন্ন নতুন অথবা অনধিক তিন বৎসরের পুরাতন মটর গাড়ি ও স্টেশন ওয়াগন, অতঃপর মটর গাড়ি বলিয়া উল্লিখিত আমদানির ক্ষেত্রে উপরি-উক্ত রেয়াত সুবিধা প্রযোজ্য হইবেঃ

তবে শর্ত থাকে যে গাড়ির বয়স ইহার চেসিস তৈরির তারিখের পরবর্তী বৎসরের প্রথম দিন হইতে গণনা করা হইবে এবং জাপান হইতে মটর গাড়ি আমদানির ক্ষেত্রে জাপানী অটোমােবাইল এ্যাসোসিয়েশন কর্তৃক প্রকাশিত চেসিসবুক অনুসারে ও অন্যান্য দেশের ক্ষেত্রে আন্তর্জাতিক খ্যাতিসম্পন্ন সার্ভেয়ার কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত সার্টিফিকেটে লিখিত গাড়ি তৈরির তারিখ অনুসারে নির্ধারিত হইবে;

(২) কেবল মাত্র Taxpayer identifications  Number প্রাপ্ত এবং ন্যূনতম ১০ লক্ষ টাকা Paid up  Capital সম্পন্ন পাবলিক বা প্রাইভেট লিমিটেড কোম্পানি উক্তরূপ মটর গাড়ি আমদানি করিতে পারিবে এবং আমদানিকৃত মটর গাড়ি আমদানিকারী কোম্পানির নামে বা অর্থায়নকারী ব্যাত্ক বা লিজিং কোম্পানির নামে ট্যাক্সিক্যাব হিসাবে রেজিট্রেশন করিতে হইবে;

তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, রেয়াতী সুবিধার অপব্যবহার হইলে আমদানিকারী কোম্পানি, সংশ্লিষ্ট অর্থায়ন ব্যাৎক বা লিজিং কোম্পানি যৌথভাবে ও এককভাবে সরকারের প্রাপ্য শুল্ক কর পরিশোধে বাধ্য থাকিবে মর্মে আমদানিকারককে সংশ্লিষ্ট শুল্ক কর্তৃপক্ষের নিকট গ্যারান্টি প্রদান করিতে হইবে;

(৩) বিআরটিএ কর্তৃক নির্ধারিত ডিজাইন, রং ও অন্যান্য বৈশিষ্ট্য সম্পন্ন ও মিটার যুক্ত অবস্থায় মটর গাড়ি আমদানি করিতে হইবে;

(৪) আমদানিকৃত মটর গাড়ির চালান শুল্কায়নের সময় আমদানিকৃত মটর গাড়ি ট্যাক্সি সার্ভিস ব্যতীত অন্য কোন উদ্দেশ্যে ব্যবহৃত হইবে না মর্মে একটি অংগীকারনামা আমদানিকারককে সংশ্লিষ্ট শুল্ক কর্তৃপক্ষের বরাবরে দাখিল করিতে হইবে;

(৫) শুল্কয়নের সময় আমদানি সংক্রান্ত সকল দলিলপত্রে “ট্যাক্সিক্যাব হিসাবে ব্যবহারের জন্য আমদানিকৃত”শব্দগুলি ঊল্লেখপূর্বক সংশ্লিষ্ট শুল্ক কর্তৃপক্ষকে সীল দিতে হইবে;

(৬) আমদানিকৃত মোটর গাড়ি শুল্কয়ন ও খালাসের পর আমদানি সংক্রান্ত প্রয়োজনীয় তথ্য শুল্ক কর্তৃপক্ষ সরাসরি বি আর টি এ-কে প্রেরণ করিবে এবং উক্ত তথ্য প্রাপ্তির পর বি আর টি এ-কে ট্যাক্সিক্যাব হিসাবে মােটরগাড়ি রেজিস্ট্রেশনের জন্য প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করিতে হইবে;

৭) সাধারণ গাড়ির উপর প্রযোজ্য স্বাভাবিক শুল্ক কর পরিশোধ এবং সেই মর্মে সংশ্লিষ্ট কমিশনার অব কাক্টমস এর প্ৰত্যয়নপত্র ব্যতিরেকে এই প্ৰজ্ঞাপনের আওতায় রেয়াতিহারে আমদানিকৃত এবং ট্যাক্সিক্যাব হিসাবে রেজিস্ট্রিকৃত কোন মোটর গাড়ি বি আর টি এ ব্যক্তিগত গাড়ি হিসাবে পুনরায় ব্লেজ্যিক্ট্রশন করিতে পারিবে না;

(৮) রেয়াতি শুল্কে আমদানিকৃত মটৰ গাড়ি হস্তান্তর করা যাইবে না " তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, কোন বিশেষ প্রয়োজনে হস্তান্তরের প্রয়োজনীয়তা দেখা দিলে বি আর টি এ কেবলমাত্র ট্যাক্সিক্যাব হিসাবে উপ-দফা (২)-এ উল্লিখিত কোন কোম্পানির নিকট মটরগাড়ি হস্তান্তরের অনুমতি প্রদান করিতে পারিবে;

আরও শর্ত থাকে যে, অনুরূপ হস্তান্তরের পূর্বে হস্তান্তর গ্রহীতা কোম্পানিতে উপ-দফা (২) এবং (৪) অনুসারে নতুনভাবে সংশ্লিষ্ট শুল্ক কর্তৃপক্ষের নিকট গ্যারান্টি ও অঙ্গীকার নামা দাখিল করিতে হইবে ৷

said SRO. Other than these two amendments the entire SRO No. 56 has been kept intact.

12. Section 30 of the Customs Act dealing with determination of the rate of duty and tariff value on imported goods, as amended in 2001, reads as follows:

"30. Date for determination of rate of duty and tariff value of imported goods—The rate of duty and tariff value applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate in force on the date a bill of entry is delivered under section 79."

Section 30A of the Customs Act which was inserted by Act 12 of 1995 deals with value and effective rate of duty and reads as follows:

"30(A) Value and effective rate of duty—Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or any decision of any court, for the purpose of section 30, the value and the rate of duty applicable to any goods shall respectively include the value as determined under section 25 and any amount of duty imposed under section 18. 18A or 18B and the amount of duty that may have become payable in consequence of the withdrawal of the whole or any part of the exemption or concession from duty whether before or after the conclusion of a contract or agreement for the sale of such goods or opening of a letter of credit in respect thereof."

13. So far sections 30 and 30A are concerned it appears that the rate of duty will be applicable to any importer on the basis of rate in force on the date of submissions of Bill of Entry.

<u>14. Now coming to the question whether the date of submission of Bills of Entry will be the basis for assessment of the rate of customs duty in these cases or not. We are to see how and when the Bills of Entry were submitted. The petitioners have taken a plea that on arrival of the goods at Benapole Port in the month of April to May 2003 the petitioners tried to submit their Bills of Entry. But for reasons best known to them the authority did not receive the same nor the authority took any step under section 82 of the Customs Act for not presenting the bills of entry within time rather by receiving the same in September/ October 2003 the respondents now cannot take the plea that since the bills of entry were presented subsequent to issuance of SRO No. 158 the duty should be assessed under the said SRO nor it could be said that since the budget was unfavourable they took the plea of vested right. Rather, upon allowing the petitioners to submit their bills of entry and receiving the same after more than four months the customs authority, it appears, allowed the extended period as provided under section 79(2) of the Act, as such, now they cannot pass any order taking advantage of SRO No. 158. Again, to see the applicability of section 30A in these cases, we are to see the scope of applicability of section 19 of Customs Act and section 14 of the VAT Act. As per the said sections, the Government has general power of exemption of customs duty and VAT under some special circumstances in public interest. To do so the Government Authority may exempt any customs duty or VAT party or wholly on any goods. As a matter of fact, the rate of customs duty enumerated by the authority under section 18 remains the same until and unless a part of it or whole of it is exempted under section 19. Actually, sections 18 and 19 are completely independent sections and one does not control the other. In these cases by incorporating the word "subject to the conditions mentioned below" in SRO No. 56 it clearly meant fulfilment of some special conditions incorporated therein to avail the exemption facilities granted under section 19 which shows that the exemption was granted to meet the immediate public demand for public transport when two stroke auto-rickshaws were decided to be withdrawn from the street of the metropolis for public interest, similar is the case under section 14 of the VAT Act.</u>

15. In Mizanur Rahman's case their Lordships found a distinction between Hannan's case and Ahamed Hossain's case on one hand and the case of Mustafizur Rahman on the other hand, although the Bills of Entry in all these cases were submitted after the subsequent SRO was issued but the Letters of Credit were opened prior to the issuance of the subsequent SRO, as in the present cases. The question arose in those cases whether the petitioners should pay duty at the rate prevalent on the date of opening of the Letter of Credit or at the rate prevalent on the date of presentation of the Bills of Entry. Their Lordships while deciding Hannan's case and Ahmed Hassain's case observed that "the importers by opening Letters of Credit earlier to withdrawal of exemption obtained a vested right which cannot be taken away by issuing a subsequent SRO. On the other hand, in the case of Mostafizur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh and 6 others, reported in 51 DLR (AD) 40, their Lordships held that the notification issued under section 19 of the Act was without any condition, limitation or restrictions and, as such, the subsequent notifications cannot have any effect when a right had vested in the importers and he had acted upon the assurance provided by that right that he would have to pay duties at the rate mentioned in the previous notification SRO". The said view was reviewed in Mizanur Rahman's case, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 149, therein their Lordships held "we therefore review our opinion expressed in that decision in 51 DLR (AD) 40 and hold that no vested right is acquired by the importer to pay sales tax and customs duty on the basis of tariff value declared by notification imposed on the date of opening of the Letter of Credit. The importer has to pay tax and duty on the basis of tariff value in-force on the date of submission of the bill of entry." But however, the view taken in Hanna's case and Ahmed Hossain's case still remains unchanged. In Mizanur Rahman's case the matter in issue was tariff value and the other 3(three) cases i.e. Hannan's case, Ahmed Hossain's case and Mostafizur Rahman's case the matter in issue was exemption of duty. In the case of Khairul Bashar (Md) and 8 others vs Collector of Customs and others reported in 50 DLR 225 the distinction between exemption under section 19 and declaration of tariff value under section 25(7) of the Customs Act was recognised. Upon noting such distinctions it has been held that the importers acquired no vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value existing at the time of opening of the Letter of Credit. So, it appears that Hannan's case and Ahmed Hossain's case are on exemption of customs duty granted under section 19 of the Customs Act which is also the subject matter of the present cases.

16. In Hannan's case it has been held that the subsequent SRO cannot destroy or take away or curtail or extinguish the vested right created on the petitioner by the earlier SRO. It was further held that the importer having already fulfilled the terms and conditions of the earlier notification he could not be deprived of the right of a concessional rate customs duty by a subsequent notification. In that case the petitioner's point was that the Government is estopped from denying the right by a subsequent notification with retrospective effect which has already been granted upon announcement of the concessional rate of duty and taxes by an earlier notification. This was nothing but the government was estopped by its own promise to do anything beyond the promise made earlier. This contention of promissory estoppel was accepted by their Lordships and accordingly, it was held that the Government cannot destroy or take away or curtail or extinguish the right created to the importers by the earlier notification. In other decision referred above the arguments of vested right was also considered. It appears from Monohar Ali's case that their Lordships observed "this Division in Mizanur Rahman's case has accepted that the submissions on vested right may be tenable in specific circumstances under section 19 of the Customs Act as to the customs duty."

<u>17. It is recognised by the superior courts that specific assurance may give some right to exist promissory estoppel. The doctrine of promissory estoppel has been called in various judgments and it has been described in various terms such as equitable estoppel, quasi estoppel or new estoppel. Justice Bhagwati in one of the judgments observed "it is not really based on the principle of estoppel but it is a doctrine involved by equity in order to prevent injustice where a promise is made by a person knowing that it would be acted on by the person to whom it is made and, in fact, it is so acted on and it is inequitable to allow the party making the promise to go back upon it". His Lordships further observed "they are really promises and promises intended to be binding intended to be acted upon and in fact, acted upon. It is an equitable principle evolved by the courts for doing justice and there is no reason why it should be given only a limited application by way of defence." Similarly, in the present cases, it appears that by SRO No. 56 the Government intended to allow a class of people having public limited company or a Private Limited Company with minimum 10 lac Taka as the paid up capital and having tax payers identification number can import taxicabs for using the same as public transport upon fulfilling certain conditions e.g. the vehicles must be black in colour, installed with catalytic converters, meter, roof sign showing the word "Taxi", etc. Further conditions were that the importers would execute undertaking that the same would be used only as taxicabs not for any other purposes. Upon fulfilling such terms and conditions if the cabs are imported then the duty above 7.5% would be exempted. So, it appears that by the said SRO, the Government has made a promise that upon fulfilment of such conditions if the importers import taxicabs they will be given the benefit as mentioned therein. The petitioners having acted upon accordingly, the Government now cannot go back upon it. If they go back it will be inequitable. So it appears that the doctrine of promissory estoppel operates when one of the parties in reliance of the promise made by the other party acts to his detriment and in such case the other party should not be allowed to go back from his promise as the same would cause injustice on the party relying upon the said promise.</u>

<u>18. Lord Denning in the "High Trees" case observed "that a promise intended to be binding, intended to be acted on and in fact, acted on, is binding so far as its terms properly apply". The contention of Lord Justice Denning in the aforesaid case and the contention of Justice Bhagwati as referred above are found to be fully applicable in the present cases. It has been observed by Lord Denning in Robertson vs Minister of Pensions (1949-1 KB 227) "the Crown cannot escape by saying that estoppels do not bind the Crown for that doctrine has long been exploded. Nor can the Crown escape by praying in aid the doctrine of executive necessity, that is, the doctrine that the Crown cannot bind itself so as to letter its future executive action". It is still held general that "the Crown is not immune from liability under the doctrine of promissory estoppel." Thus the promise made by the Government through the National Board of Revenue, the supreme authority of collecting Revenue of the country, by issuing SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999 cannot now come back from the said promise because of the subsequent amendment incorporated by SRO No. 158, of 2003. It may be noted here that by the subsequent SRO No. 158 the amendment as regards exemption of duty has been reduced and a bottom limit has been fixed by incorporating taxi cabs being not less than 1301 CC meaning any person importing Motor car or taxicab below 1300 CC and above 2000 CC would be liable to pay customs duty on the regular rate i.e. import of taxicabs from 1301 CC to 2000 CC upon fulfilling the conditions contained in the SRO No. 56 may get the benefit of exemption of duty above 15%. This amendment appears to be shifting from the promise already made in the earlier SRO. The petitioners having opened the Letters of Credit, and shipment having been made prior to issuance of the subsequent SRO upon fulfilling all the terms and conditions including the inspections of the vehicles under sections 25A and 25B by the approved PSI agents they have acted in accordance with the conditions of the SRO and, as such, the promisor, i.e. the Government, now cannot fall back and ask for payment of customs duty on any other basis other than SRO No. 56. Under such circumstances it appears that the position of the petitioners in the present cases are as such that the situation has taken place, arising out of promise made under section 19 of the Act, to exempt the imported taxicab from assessing or paying taxes and duties under special circumstances. Thus the importers having acted on the promise made by the government under section 19 of the Act to avail the facilities granted in SRO No. 56 on compliance of all the terms and conditions incorporated therein, the government, rather the respondents, are estopped from going back from that promise rather the same is binding on them. The principle of promissory estoppel and fair action are applicable to the facts of the case and the respondent are debarred having no justification in law to supersede earlier notification which has to remain in force without limitation to time. Thus subsequent notification to the extent it superseded the earlier one will have no binding effect in such special cases concerning public interests, this view finds support in the case of Collector of Customs vs Abul Hossain reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 and in the case of Collector of Customs and others vs Ahmed Hossain and others 48 DLR (AD) 199.</u>

19. The view taken in Mustafizur Rahman's case thought reviewed and set aside in Mizanur Rahman's case but the view taken in Hannan's case has not been set aside or reviewed in any other decision. Though it is submitted from some quarter that the principle enunciated in Hannan's case if especiality and exception of its own but we find that the principle annunciated therein is related to exemption of duty under section 19 in some special circumstances which we find similarity with present cases. In the said case the government allowed some incentive to the genuine importers to import sugar within a specific time to meet the urgent need in the market as there were scarcities of the same in 1984. Similarly, in the present case the Government by SRO No. 56 asked a class of people to import taxicabs upon fulfilment of certain conditions enunciated therein, to meet the urgent need of filling up the vacuum in public transport created when two strokes 3(three) wheeler auto-rickshaws were withdrawn from the street of the Metropolitan area for environmental degradation by a Government order. To meet such vacuum and urgent need of meeting the cry of the public transportation, SRO No. 56 was issued. So if it is submitted that the decision in Hannan's case is an exception of its own the same principle also applies in these cases. Strictly speaking, when it appears that the concerned SRO was issued for a particular purpose and for public interest and the importers having fulfilled all the terms and conditions incorporated in the said SRO upon obtaining loans from the commercial banks and upon opening the Letters of Credit through the concerned banks, the Government or the customs authority cannot be allowed to work inconsistently, whimsically and capriciously to the prejudice of the importer who acted accordingly and fulfilled the conditions of the said SRO issued at an earlier point of time. The view finds support in the case of Chairman, Board of Investment and others vs Bay Trawling Limited and others, reported in 51 DLR (AD) 79 Moreover, a person is entitled to claim benefit under a SRO wherein the authority has promised such exemption if he suffers loss for no fault of his own. But he is not entitled to claim such benefit in a situation where the person would not suffer any loss by such payment as a result of his being able to realise the same from a third party or third person wherefrom such loss could be realised by him. Reason being that the person who has suffered no loss by making an unauthorised payment to another person cannot get refund of the same from that person as he was able to make good the loss by shifting the burden of the same on the shoulders of another person. The petitioners in these writ petitions being Private Limited Companies upon importing taxicabs, undertook to use the same as taxicabs for the purpose of public transportation they cannot shift the burden of payment of extra duty on a subsequent purchaser and, as such, the loss incurred would be completely of their own. Under such situation it is discouraged that the extra duty should be realised from them. This view finds support in the case of Tamanna Steel Galvanizing Industry Ltd vs Bangladesh and others, reported in 50 DLR 8.

<u>20. Now coming to the question of maintainability of the writ petitions when the statutory relief is available by way of appeal under section 193 of the Customs Act not being availed of by the petitioners instead the petitioners have come before this Court under the writ jurisdiction without availing the said forum. In all these Rules it appears that the petitioner have challenged the impugned order passed by the authority directing to assess the customs duty on the consignments at a rate fixed by SRO No. 158 dated 12-6-2003 instead of exempted rate under SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999. Here the question arises as to the applicability of SRO No. 158 dated 12-6-2003 which is a Statutory Regulatory Order passed under the authority of section 19 of the Act and section 14 of the VAT Act that means here the question of interpretation of law as well as the applicability and the authority of the SRO arises. It is the settled principle that where the vires of Statute of statutory provision is under question the remedy can be availed of under the Writ Jurisdiction as provided in Article 102 of the Constitution though alternative remedy having not been availed. In such a case the alternative remedy is neither efficacious nor adequate and where the wrong complained is so inextricably mixed up the High Court Division may, for the prevention of public injury and vindication of public justice, examine such complaint. This view has been taken by our Appellate Division in the case of Dhaka Warehouse Ltd vs Assistant Collector of Customs and others, reported in 1991 BLD (AD) 327 which has also been noticed in Mizanur Rahman 's case. In the present cases the question relates to interpretation of sections 19 and 30 of the Act. Thus, in our opinion, availing the writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution under such situation is permissible. Ordinarily writ petition against an order of assessment of customs duty or imposition of fine is not maintainable and remedy of appeal is to be availed against the same. But in the present cases the assessment having not been made and no question of imposition of any fine being there rather the only question for determination in these rules is whether SRO No. 158 is applicable under the facts and circumstances of the cases. Our opinion is that the present writ petitions are maintainable because the remedy provided in the Act would not be equally efficacious to bar the jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. Thus, in not availing the alternative remedy there is no bar under facts and circumstances of these writ petitions to vindicate the grievances under the writ jurisdiction.</u>

<u>21. So far the contention of the learned Additional Attorney-General as to maturity of the Writ Petitions is concerned it is found that by refusing to assess customs duty on the basis of SRO No. 56 and directing to assess duties on the basis of SRO No. 158 the Customs Authority has taken the final decision for assessment and, as such, the Writ Petitions are not prematured.</u>

<u>22. Under the facts and circumstances stated above and the decision referred to above, only question left out to see is, whether section 30A is applicable in these cases in such a situation. The language of section 30A clearly shows that for the purpose of imposition of duty and exemption of duty section 30 will be applicable under any circumstances generally. But in a case where the situation of present nature arises and the government having amended the benefit given under SRO No. 56 restricting the same to certain limit without any prior notice in general to the public even after continuation of the previous SRO for more than 4 years the action taken by the government appears to be inconsistent and capricious prejudicing the persons who had already acted upon on the basis of the previous SRO. Under such situation, in our view, section 30A will not be applicable. In fact, upon reading the language of section 30A it appears that the rate of duty is to be ascertained by taking into account any duty imposed under section 18 or any exemption or concession of duty granted under the Act. Thus, in the present cases considering the speciality of the facts and circumstances sections 30 or 30A should be read independent of section 19 and accordingly, any exemption granted under section 19 should not be affected by section 30 or 30A of the Act or the date of submission of Bills of Entry. The above issues were not placed and argued in writ petition No. 4603 of 2003 and, as such, these rules being decided in favour of the petitioners as per reasoning stated above, we do not want to make any comment on the said judgment.</u>

23. Considering the facts and circumstances of the cases and the decisions stated above, we are of the view that all the rules succeed and accordingly, the impugned orders in each of the writ petitions are hereby declared to have been passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

24. In the result, the Rules in all the 8 (eight) writ petitions being Writ Petition Nos. 6433-6439 of 2003 and 5950 of 2003 are made absolute.

25. The respondents are hereby directed to assess the customs duty and other charges for the petitioner's imported consignments as per SRO No. 56 dated 16-3-1999 which was in force at the time of opening of the Letters of Credit and release the Taxicabs within 1(one) month from the date of receipt of this order.

26. The Bank Guarantee furnished by the writ petitioner in Writ Petition No. 5950 of 2003 is liable to be released and the respondents are accordingly, directed to do the needful in this regard within 1(one) month from the date of receipt of this order.

Considering the circumstances, there will be no order as to cost.
